title: Circuit Breakers & Bulkheads
subtitle: Watch one slow dependency drain a whole service, then watch a breaker, a bulkhead and a fallback stop it.
learn: Why a slow dependency is more dangerous than a dead one
How a circuit breaker moves between closed, open and half-open
How failing fast frees threads and gives the sick service room to recover
How bulkheads cap the damage one dependency can do to shared pools
How to pick a fallback that degrades the page instead of breaking it

steps.title: A nice-to-have takes down the page
steps.body: Each product page on the Shop API calls Recommendations (a nice-to-have 'you may also like' row) and Payments (essential). Traffic is 500 requests per second and the Shop API has 200 worker threads. Normally recommendations answer in 40 ms, so only about 12 threads are busy at any moment. What happens when that one optional service stops answering?
steps.idea: A dependency you could live without can still sink you if you wait on it.
steps.caption: Healthy baseline: 500 req/s, about 12 busy threads.

steps.title: Slow is worse than down
steps.body: Recommendations now hang for 30 seconds before failing. A dead service refuses connections instantly and the caller moves on, but a slow one holds a thread. By Little's law, 500 requests per second times 30 seconds wants 15,000 threads, and we only have 200. The pool is full in under half a second. Now even checkout pages, which never needed recommendations, queue for a thread and time out.
steps.idea: Slow calls hold resources; resource exhaustion turns one sick dependency into a full outage (a cascading failure).
steps.caption: Threads pile up waiting on Recommendations.

steps.title: Closed: counting quietly
steps.body: A circuit breaker is a small wrapper around calls to one dependency. Like the electrical kind, 'closed' means current flows: every call goes through. The breaker watches the recent results in a rolling window, say the last 10 seconds, and counts failures and timeouts. In this normal state it adds almost no cost, just a counter.
steps.idea: Closed is the normal state: pass everything through and keep score.
steps.caption: Breaker closed: calls pass, outcomes are counted.

steps.title: Trip: closed becomes open
steps.body: Suppose the rule is: with at least 20 calls in the window, open the breaker if 50% or more failed. A short per-call timeout (here 500 ms) turns hangs into counted failures within about a second. Once the threshold is crossed, the breaker trips to open. Thresholds are rules of thumb you tune from real traffic, not magic numbers.
steps.idea: A timeout makes slowness countable; the failure rate threshold decides when to trip.
steps.caption: Failures cross 50%: the breaker trips open.

steps.title: Open: reject in a millisecond
steps.body: While open, the breaker does not call Recommendations at all. It answers immediately with an error that the Shop API can handle. Each request now holds a thread for about a millisecond instead of 500 ms or more, so threads drain back to normal. The sick service also stops receiving 500 calls per second, which gives it quiet time to recover instead of drowning under retries.
steps.idea: Failing fast protects the caller's threads and gives the callee room to heal.
steps.caption: Calls rejected locally; Recommendations is left alone.

steps.title: Degrade instead of erroring
steps.body: A rejected call still needs an answer. For optional data, the Shop API serves a fallback: here a cached list of the 20 most popular items, refreshed every few minutes. Shoppers see a slightly less personal row, and nothing else changes. Choose fallbacks that are cheap and independent of the failing service: a cache, a default value, or hiding the widget. Do not fall back to calling another fragile service.
steps.idea: Graceful degradation means a worse answer is returned instead of no answer.
steps.caption: Breaker serves popular items from cache.

steps.title: Half-open: let a few probes through
steps.body: Staying open forever would be a bug, so after a cool-down (say 30 seconds) the breaker goes half-open. It lets a small number of trial calls through, for example 3, and holds back everyone else. If the probes succeed, the breaker closes and traffic resumes. If any fails, it snaps back to open and the cool-down starts again.
steps.idea: Half-open tests recovery with a trickle so a healing service is not hit by the full crowd at once.
steps.caption: Probes succeed: breaker closes, recs return.

steps.title: Bulkheads cap the blast radius
steps.body: Ships have watertight compartments so one leak cannot sink the whole hull. Do the same with pools: give Recommendations its own limit of 20 concurrent calls out of the 200 threads. If it hangs again before the breaker trips, only those 20 slots fill; extra recommendation calls are rejected at once. Payments keeps its own pool, so checkout carries on untouched.
steps.idea: A bulkhead limits how much of a shared resource any one dependency may consume.
steps.caption: Recs pool full and rejecting; payments unaffected.

steps.title: Where breakers go wrong
steps.body: Breakers trip on server errors and timeouts, not on client mistakes such as a 404 or 400. A breaker per dependency, per instance, only sees its own slice of traffic; low-traffic callers may never reach the 20-call minimum. A threshold that is too tight opens on a blip, too loose reacts late. And a fallback that is silently stale needs alerts, so people notice the breaker is open. Retry logic belongs outside an open breaker, not through it.
steps.idea: Breakers need sensible failure definitions, minimum volume, a visible state and a harmless fallback.
steps.caption: Tuning and monitoring decide whether it helps.

steps.title: Fail fast, isolate, degrade
steps.body: A slow dependency exhausts threads, so use timeouts to make slowness a countable failure. A breaker moves closed to open to half-open to stop calling a sick service and to test recovery gently. A bulkhead gives each dependency its own capped pool. A fallback turns a rejected call into a lesser but working answer. Together they keep one broken optional feature from becoming a total outage.
steps.idea: Timeouts detect, breakers stop, bulkheads contain, fallbacks soften.
steps.caption: Page stays up while recommendations are down.

quiz.q: Recommendations goes from 40 ms to hanging for 30 s. Why is that usually more dangerous than it simply being down?
options: Hung calls hold threads and connections, so the caller runs out of capacity
Hung calls use more network bandwidth than refused ones
A hung service writes corrupted data into shared databases
The load balancer removes the caller from rotation immediately
quiz.why: A dead service refuses quickly and frees the thread. A slow one keeps each thread occupied, and at 500 req/s the pool of 200 fills in well under a second.

quiz.q: A breaker is open. What does it do with a new call?
options: Queues it until the dependency recovers
Retries it against the dependency three times
Rejects it immediately, or returns a fallback, without calling the dependency
Sends it to the dependency but ignores the response
quiz.why: Open means the dependency is not contacted. The call returns at once with an error or fallback, which frees the thread and relieves the dependency.

quiz.q: Why does the half-open state allow only a few probe calls rather than all traffic?
options: To measure latency percentiles accurately
To avoid hitting a barely recovered service with full load and knocking it over again
Because breakers cannot count above three calls
To keep the cache warm
quiz.why: A recovering service may be fragile. A trickle of trial calls tests health cheaply, and a single failure reopens the breaker.

quiz.q: How is a bulkhead different from a circuit breaker?
options: A bulkhead reacts to failure rates; a breaker only counts threads
They are two names for the same mechanism
A bulkhead caps concurrent use of a resource per dependency, whether or not it is failing; a breaker reacts to observed failures
A bulkhead only works for databases
quiz.why: The bulkhead is a static limit that works even before failures are measured. The breaker is dynamic and based on outcomes. They are used together.

quiz.q: The checkout 'charge card' call fails. Which fallback is most appropriate?
options: Show a cached list of popular items
Report the payment as successful and reconcile later without telling the user
Tell the user clearly that payment could not be completed and let them retry
Silently skip payment and ship the order
quiz.why: Fallbacks suit optional data. Essential, money-moving operations must not pretend to succeed; the right degradation is an honest error or a retry-safe path.

cheatsheet.def: Normal state. Calls pass through while the breaker counts recent failures in a rolling window.
Tripped state. Calls are rejected immediately or served a fallback; the dependency is left alone.
After a cool-down, a few probe calls test recovery. Success closes the breaker; failure reopens it.
Rule of thumb: trip at 50% failures over 20+ calls in 10 s, stay open 30 s, 3 probes. Tune with real traffic.
A breaker needs timeouts to turn hangs into failures it can count. Keep timeouts short.
A per-dependency cap on concurrent calls, threads or connections, so one dependency cannot consume the shared pool.
A cheap substitute answer: cache, default, or hiding the feature. Never use for money-moving writes.
Count timeouts and 5xx errors. Do not count 4xx client errors; they are not a sign the dependency is unhealthy.
